clue.text: Prosecuting officer and copper brought into service in capital city

indicators.note: something brought into a place ends up inside it, so one piece sits within another

blocks.note: a district attorney, the American public prosecutor
a church service
Cu is the chemical symbol for copper

explanation.surface: A prosecutor and a policeman are drafted into some duty in a nation's capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copper' looks like a policeman but is the metal, and the service is a church one. DA is the American district attorney.
explanation.definitionFit: Damascus is the capital of Syria, one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities.

clue.text: Adult, on the outside mostly adroit, is handicapped in some way

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the last letter is dropped
a word on the outside wraps around another, holding it within

blocks.note: deft means skilful
A is the film certificate for adult

explanation.surface: A grown-up who appears skilful outwardly but has a disability.
explanation.walkthrough: DEFT loses its last letter, and DEF goes around A.
explanation.definitionFit: Being unable to hear is one kind of disability, so it fits a vague physical impairment.

clue.text: Flier given sort of test on helicopter initially

indicators.note: initially points to taking only the opening letter of the word

blocks.note: the MOT is Britain's annual roadworthiness test for vehicles
its opening letter

explanation.surface: A pilot sitting some kind of exam on a helicopter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flier' suggests a pilot; it is an insect.
explanation.definitionFit: A moth is a winged insect, and anything that flies can be called a flier.

clue.text: Not prone to be among students up in English

indicators.note: loosely, the leading letter is drawn from among the students

blocks.note: its opening letter
taken as written; up is also at university
taken as written
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: Someone not inclined to join the university crowd studying English.
explanation.walkthrough: A loose parse: S, then UP IN, then E. In British use, to be up is to be at university, which explains the students.
explanation.definitionFit: Supine means lying face upward, the opposite of prone, which is lying face down.

clue.text: Exploit admitted by erstwhile England bowler creates drama

indicators.note: what is admitted is let inside, so one word goes within the other

blocks.note: Derek Underwood, the Kent and England spin bowler of the 1960s and 70s
to milk is to exploit

explanation.surface: A former cricketer takes advantage of the situation and makes a scene.
explanation.walkthrough: Derek Underwood was a famous England cricket bowler; 'exploit' is a verb here, not a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Under Milk Wood is Dylan Thomas's radio play, a drama for voices about a Welsh village.

clue.text: Villain, twisted inside, about to become a sailor

indicators.note: twisted and turned about tell us the word's letters are rearranged, here by swapping its ends

blocks.note: a rascal is a rogue or villain

explanation.surface: A villain, warped inside, turns himself around and goes to sea.
explanation.walkthrough: The middle ASCA stays put while the outer R and L change places, turning a rogue into a seaman.
explanation.definitionFit: A lascar is an Indian or Southeast Asian seaman, historically crewing European merchant ships.

clue.text: A medic attending university student, six-footer not confined to bed

blocks.note: taken as written
MB, Bachelor of Medicine, a doctor's degree
U is the abbreviation for university
L for learner, as on a British learner driver's plate
an insect has six legs, so an ant is a six-footer

explanation.surface: A doctor visiting a student and a very tall person who is able to walk about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Six-footer' suggests a tall person, but it is a six-legged insect.
explanation.definitionFit: Ambulant describes a patient able to walk around rather than being bedridden.

clue.text: A hundred eat pig cooked in old-time English dish

indicators.note: cooking transforms ingredients, so the letters are worked into a new shape

blocks.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred
taken as written
taken as written
O is the abbreviation for old
T is the abbreviation for time
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: A hundred people tuck into roast pork in a traditional English meal.
explanation.walkthrough: C leads, then EAT PIG plus O, T and E are mixed together.
explanation.definitionFit: Cottage pie is a traditional British dish of minced beef topped with mashed potato.

clue.text: A sign of something wrong in family member? Rest is the answer

indicators.note: in places the sign inside the other word

blocks.note: a relative
a cross marks an error
taken as written

explanation.surface: Signs of trouble in a relative; the remedy is a break.
explanation.walkthrough: The cross and the A go in together, splitting the relative after its fourth letter. The surface 'answer' is only the solution to the trouble.
explanation.definitionFit: Relaxation is time off from work or stress, the same as taking a break.

clue.text: Poles separated? There's clue in that!

definitions.text: Poles separated? There's clue in that!

blocks.note: surface reading: Polish people, or magnetic poles, being kept apart
setter's reading: points on opposite sides of the globe, as far apart as the North and South Poles

explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation teases that the clue itself is the hint: places diametrically opposite on the Earth are separated as far as poles are.
explanation.definitionFit: Antipodes are places diametrically opposite each other on the globe, like the two geographic poles.

clue.text: Rattle cut in half by silicon?

definitions.note: silicon is an example, signalled by the question mark

blocks.note: semi means half
Sir Simon Rattle, the British orchestra conductor

explanation.surface: A rattle sawn in two by silicon.
explanation.walkthrough: Rattle looks like a baby's toy but is the conductor; 'half' comes before him.
explanation.definitionFit: Silicon is the classic example of a material whose electrical conductivity lies between conductor and insulator.

clue.text: Semi-star seen in leaf of climbing plant

indicators.note: semi means half, so only the front half of the star's name is kept

blocks.note: the first five letters of Betelgeuse, the red giant in Orion

explanation.surface: Half a star turns up on a vine leaf.
explanation.walkthrough: Betelgeuse has ten letters; the half-star is its first five.
explanation.definitionFit: Betel leaves come from a climbing pepper vine and are chewed with areca nut across South Asia.

clue.text: French writer makes rural dean, MA, frightfully cross

indicators.note: frightfully suggests things thrown into disorder, so the letters are mixed up

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
a cross is the letter X

explanation.surface: A country clergyman with a master's degree is terribly angry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cross' looks like the dean's mood but supplies the letter X for the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: Andre Malraux was a French novelist, author of Man's Fate, and later de Gaulle's culture minister.

clue.text: Some porn he circulated could account for sexual arousal

indicators.note: things circulated are passed around and mixed, so the letters change order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Smut a man passed around might be what turns people on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some' looks like it introduces hidden letters, but it is part of the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: Pheromones are chemical signals released by animals that trigger responses such as attraction in others.

clue.text: Tiny POW? May be observed in a cave

definitions.text: May be observed in a cave

blocks.note: a Stalag was a German camp for prisoners of war
a mite is a tiny creature or child

explanation.surface: A little prisoner of war glimpsed hiding underground.
explanation.walkthrough: The POW camp comes first, then the small one.
explanation.definitionFit: A stalagmite is a mineral column rising from a cave floor, built up by dripping water.

clue.text: What that enemy harbours?

indicators.note: to harbour is to hold within, so the phrase before it contains the letters

blocks.note: spans the end of that and the start of enemy

explanation.surface: A question about what feelings a foe nurses.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the wordplay and the definition: the letters sit inside the words, and an enemy does nurse this feeling.
explanation.definitionFit: Hostility or loathing is the feeling a foe nurses toward an opponent.

clue.text: Club being given new temporary accommodation makes one unhappy

definitions.note: the clue's makes one unhappy describes a state of dissatisfaction, a noun

blocks.note: a disco is a dance club
N is the abbreviation for new
a tent is a shelter put up for a short stay

explanation.surface: A nightclub forced into makeshift premises leaves someone grumpy.
explanation.definitionFit: Discontent is a state of dissatisfaction, the feeling of someone who is not happy.

clue.text: Achieved aim to include six in share-out

indicators.note: to include something is to hold it within, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: did plus end, achieved plus goal
VI is six in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: Someone hit their target by getting six in a distribution.
explanation.definitionFit: A dividend is a portion of company profits paid out to shareholders, a distribution.

clue.text: Jovial ruler has first spin in charge

blocks.note: to roll is to turn over and over
i/c is the standard abbreviation for in charge
a king is a monarch

explanation.surface: A cheerful monarch takes the first turn at being in command.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Has first' places the spin and the in-charge pieces ahead of the ruler.
explanation.definitionFit: Rollicking means boisterously cheerful and exuberant, close in sense to jolly.

clue.text: Dissolute type with nothing to gain?

blocks.note: to win is to gain
zero, shaped like the letter O

explanation.surface: A wastrel who has nothing to get out of life.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nothing to gain' reads as despair, but splits into the nought tacked on the end of a win.
explanation.definitionFit: A wino is a habitual drunk, often homeless, the very picture of a dissipated person.

clue.text: Three separate articles submitted by woman

blocks.note: an, the and a, three articles one after another

explanation.surface: A woman hands in three distinct pieces of writing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Articles' suggests pieces of writing but means grammatical articles.
explanation.definitionFit: Anthea is a female first name, so it stands for any woman as crosswords often allow.

clue.text: Man, long quiet, getting drunk and boastful

indicators.note: a drunk staggers about, so the letters reel into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A long-silent man has a few drinks and starts bragging.
explanation.definitionFit: Magniloquent means using lofty, grandiose language, the speech of a braggart showing off.

clue.text: Knave in a suit and I have brief dance

blocks.note: J is the card abbreviation for jack, the knave
I've is the short form of I have

explanation.surface: A rogue in a suit and I share a quick dance.
explanation.walkthrough: The knave is a playing card, in one of the four suits; 'brief' shortens I have.
explanation.definitionFit: Jive is a lively jazz-age partner dance, a form of swing.

clue.text: Relish turning roof of shelter through 90 degrees

indicators.note: the roof is the top letter of a down entry, and turning it on its side changes it into a different letter

blocks.note: a nest is a bird's shelter

explanation.surface: Enjoying turning a roof a quarter turn.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry the roof is the first letter. Turn N a quarter turn and it becomes Z.
explanation.definitionFit: Zest means keen enjoyment or gusto, as does relish.

clue.text: Instruction prescribing "-ize" brings a rumpus

blocks.note: a style editor's rule meaning use -ize, not -ise

explanation.surface: A copy editor's spelling ruling causes an uproar.
explanation.walkthrough: An editor insisting on -ize would write 'no -ise', which read as one word is a din.
explanation.definitionFit: A rumpus is a loud commotion or disturbance, which is what racket and din describe.

clue.text: The missus doubly offering support in bed

blocks.note: 'my old dutch' is Cockney for one's wife, from rhyming slang duchess of Fife
the missus a second time, now as plain wife

explanation.surface: A wife does double duty propping someone up in bed.
explanation.walkthrough: The missus is taken twice: once as Cockney slang, once straight.
explanation.definitionFit: A Dutch wife is a long bolster or open cane frame used in hot climates to rest the limbs on at night.

clue.text: Unreliable date, yes? Not 'e!

definitions.note: read whole: a date who is not unreliable, a regular partner

indicators.note: something unreliable cannot be trusted to stay in order, so the letters are reshuffled
not tells us a letter is to be left out of the fodder

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
the dropped-aitch he is just the letter to remove

explanation.surface: Is this date a flaky one? Not him, surely!
explanation.walkthrough: Remove one E from DATE YES and rearrange. Read whole, the clue denies that the date is unreliable: a dependable regular partner.
explanation.definitionFit: A steady is a regular boyfriend or girlfriend, someone dependable you go out with consistently.

clue.text: Decorate set of holy books with gold title at front

blocks.note: or is the heraldic word for gold
a title is a name
NT is the New Testament

explanation.surface: Adorning a volume of scripture with a gilt heading on its cover.
explanation.definitionFit: To ornament something is to adorn or embellish it, a verb as well as a noun.
